playbook_sections.text: EDR/behavioral rule flags shadow-copy deletion (T1490) or mass file-rename/ encryption activity across shares (T1486) - T1490 firing FIRST, before mass changes begin, is the highest-value early-warning signal this alert type is designed to catch.

Isolate the affected host(s) from the network immediately - do not power off (this destroys memory forensics and can trigger some ransomware's "wipe on shutdown" behavior). If shadow-copy deletion is still in progress, disable/kill that process first.

/api/playbooks/web_application_attack.attack: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application) - Initial Access (TA0001). Note this is the same top-level technique as vulnerability.md's Vulnerability alert type - ATT&CK's technique catalog models the adversary's action (exploiting a public-facing app), not the specific vulnerability class (SQLi/XSS/directory traversal are OWASP/CWE categories, not separate ATT&CK sub-techniques), so the same ID is the honest answer for both rather than forcing an artificial distinction. The practical difference here is that this alert type reflects an attempt actually observed against the application (via WAF/app logs), not just an unpatched exposure.

blocks.text: WAF or application log flags a known attack pattern (SQL injection, XSS probe, directory traversal) against a specific endpoint.

Add the source IP to the WAF blocklist and tighten the matching rule if it's a known attack class; if the app itself is confirmed exploitable, restrict access (e.g. VPN-only) while a fix is prepared.
Patch or add a virtual patch for the underlying vulnerability if the application code is confirmed exploitable.
Restore normal access once the patch/virtual patch is verified; invalidate any sessions or data affected by a confirmed successful exploitation.
Close as Blocked if the WAF stopped it with no evidence of compromise; if it reached the app, treat the underlying code defect as the real root cause, not just this one attack attempt.

/api/playbooks/data_exfiltration.title: Data Exfiltration
/api/playbooks/data_exfiltration.attack: T1567.002 (Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage) - Exfiltration (TA0010), for the "uploaded to external cloud storage/ personal email" pattern this alert type is built around.

blocks.text: DLP or proxy/CASB rule flags an outbound transfer to an external cloud-storage domain or personal email account, especially one matching sensitive-data patterns (PII, financials, source code).

Identify the destination and confirm it is not a sanctioned business service (a personal Dropbox/Gmail account vs. an approved corporate cloud tenant materially changes the response). Determine what data left: file names/types and volume.

Block the outbound channel at the proxy/CASB; suspend the source account's outbound access pending review. Do not tip off the user if insider intent is suspected (see insider_threat.md for the closely related decision tree).
Request a takedown from the destination cloud provider if the data was confirmed sensitive and the transfer unauthorized.
Restore normal access once cleared, or hand off to HR/Legal-led process if substantiated - preserve proxy/DLP logs and the affected endpoint's file-access history as evidence throughout.

Escalate to Legal/Privacy if regulated data (PII, PCI, PHI) was confirmed involved; otherwise close as Contained once the channel is blocked, and note whether this destination category (personal cloud storage) needs a standing block rather than per-incident handling.

/api/playbooks/suspicious_login.name: suspicious_login
/api/playbooks/suspicious_login.title: Suspicious Login
/api/playbooks/suspicious_login.attack: T1078 (Valid Accounts) - spans Initial Access (TA0001), Persistence (TA0003), Privilege Escalation (TA0004), and Defense Evasion (TA0005), since a valid but compromised account can be used at any of those stages; for the SSO/cloud-login impossible-travel pattern specifically, sub-technique T1078.004 (Cloud Accounts) applies.

blocks.text: Impossible-travel rule (same account, two logins, physically implausible elapsed time) or a new-device/new-location flag never seen for this account before.

Confirm impossibility/implausibility of the pattern against known device/location history - and check whether an MFA push was approved (MFA-fatigue attacks rely on the user approving without noticing, which does not confirm legitimacy).
Force an immediate password reset and re-authentication with MFA for the affected account; revoke active sessions/tokens issued during the suspicious window.

Review the account's session activity between the two logins for any data access, forwarding-rule changes, or config changes made by the attacker if the account was compromised - remove any such changes.
Restore normal access once the account is confirmed clean; de-register any unrecognized device involved.
Close as Contained if no unauthorized activity occurred during the window; if MFA fatigue was the vector, consider number-matching MFA instead of simple push approval.

/api/playbooks/brute_force.name: brute_force
/api/playbooks/brute_force.title: Brute Force / Credential Attack
/api/playbooks/brute_force.attack: T1110 (Brute Force) - Credential Access (TA0006). Where the pattern is many accounts each tried a few times rather than one account tried many times, see sub-technique T1110.003 (Password Spraying) specifically.

blocks.text: Authentication-log threshold alert: repeated failed logins for one account from one source (T1110 classic pattern) or a low-and-slow spread of failed attempts across many accounts from one or few sources (T1110.003 password-spray pattern) - the two need different detection logic, since a per-account threshold alone misses spraying.

Determine which pattern this is (single-account brute force vs. spray) and whether any attempt succeeded. Review the targeted account(s)' recent successful logins for signs the attacker eventually got in.

Block the source IP(s) at the perimeter firewall/VPN gateway. For a spray pattern, consider a temporary global lockout-threshold tightening rather than only blocking the observed source, since spray sources often rotate.
If any login succeeded, treat the account as compromised: force a password reset and review for any changes made during the compromised session (mail rules, new MFA devices registered, etc.).
Enroll the targeted account(s) in MFA if not already enrolled; restore normal login availability once the source is blocked and no successful compromise is confirmed.
Close as Contained if no successful login from the attacking source is found; otherwise document how the attempt bypassed existing lockout thresholds and adjust them.

/api/playbooks/insider_threat.name: insider_threat
/api/playbooks/insider_threat.title: Insider Threat / Data Exfiltration
/api/playbooks/insider_threat.attack: T1052.001 (Exfiltration Over Physical Medium: Exfiltration over USB) - Exfiltration (TA0010), for the removable-media pattern this alert type is built around. Where the pattern is instead unusual access to data outside a user's normal job function (no physical medium involved), there is no single precise ATT&CK technique - ATT&CK models adversary tradecraft, not user-behavior/role-based anomalies, so this part of the analysis leans on UEBA-style reasoning rather than a technique ID.

blocks.text: DLP or endpoint policy flags data movement to removable media, or a UEBA-style rule flags access/volume outside a user's normal pattern.

Confirm data volume, destination, and business justification with the user's manager before assuming malicious intent - this alert type has a real false-positive rate against legitimate but unusual work (e.g. an approved offboarding data handoff).
If unjustified, suspend the user's access pending investigation. Do not tip off the user prematurely if deliberate intent is suspected, since that risks destruction of evidence.

Not typically applicable unless the removable media/destination can be recovered and the copied data confirmed deleted - coordinate with Legal on this, since eradication here often means legal/administrative action, not a technical fix.
Restore the user's access once cleared, or proceed to HR/Legal-led offboarding if substantiated - preserve forensic evidence (do not wipe the device) throughout.
Document chain of custody for all evidence collected; if this was a policy gap (e.g. removable media should have been disabled for this role), close that gap.

/api/playbooks/ransomware_indicator.name: ransomware_indicator
/api/playbooks/ransomware_indicator.title: Ransomware Indicator
/api/playbooks/ransomware_indicator.attack: T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact) - Impact (TA0040), for the end-state this alert type warns of. The specific precursor behavior this alert type is built around - shadow-copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic immediately before mass file changes - maps precisely to T1490 (Inhibit System Recovery) - Impact (TA0040); this is the exact, verified technique (confirmed directly against the current attack.mitre.org page, which documents "vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet" as the canonical example, used by WannaCry, BlackCat, Conti, LockBit and others).

blocks.text: EDR/behavioral rule flags shadow-copy deletion (T1490) or mass file-rename/ encryption activity across shares (T1486) - T1490 firing FIRST, before mass changes begin, is the highest-value early-warning signal this alert type is designed to catch.

Determine blast radius immediately: which hosts/shares show the same pattern. This is time-critical - ransomware spreads faster than most other alert types on this list, so Analysis and Containment often happen in parallel rather than sequentially.

Isolate the affected host(s) from the network immediately - do not power off (this destroys memory forensics and can trigger some ransomware's "wipe on shutdown" behavior). If shadow-copy deletion is still in progress, disable/kill that process first.
Identify and disable the responsible process; confirm no other host on the same subnet is still executing the same pattern before considering eradication complete.

Restore affected files from the most recent clean backup once the host is confirmed contained - verify backup integrity before restoring, since some ransomware campaigns specifically target backup infrastructure first.
Treat every T1490 (shadow-copy deletion) sighting as a major-incident trigger going forward, even in isolation - waiting for confirmed encryption before escalating costs valuable containment time.

/api/playbooks/c2_beaconing.name: c2_beaconing
/api/playbooks/c2_beaconing.title: C2 Beaconing
/api/playbooks/c2_beaconing.attack: T1071 (Application Layer Protocol) - Command and Control (TA0011) for periodic outbound connections generally; where domain-generation-algorithm domains are involved specifically, T1568.002 (Dynamic Resolution: Domain Generation Algorithms) - Command and Control (TA0011) applies (confirmed directly against the current attack.mitre.org page).

blocks.text: Network sensor flags periodic outbound connections with regular beacon-interval timing (T1071), or DNS requests to a newly-registered/algorithmically-generated domain (T1568.002 DGA pattern).

Identify the initiating process and any dropped payloads or scheduled tasks that establish persistence; check other hosts for connections to the same domain/IP or a matching beacon-interval pattern, which would indicate lateral spread.
Block the destination domain/IP at the firewall/DNS layer; isolate the beaconing host from the network via EDR while preserving it for forensic capture (do not wipe before capturing).

Remove the beaconing process and any persistence mechanism it installed; for DGA-based C2, block the DGA pattern via threat-intel feed rather than only the currently-observed domain, since new domains will register on the same algorithm.
Reimage the host once forensics are captured; close as Contained only after confirming no other host still beacons to the same destination or matching pattern.
If egress filtering would have caught this sooner (non-standard port, unapproved destination), tighten egress rules rather than relying solely on beacon-pattern detection next time.

/api/playbooks/malware.name: malware
/api/playbooks/malware.title: Malware
/api/playbooks/malware.attack: T1204.002 (User Execution: Malicious File) - Execution (TA0002). Where the process observed is a known living-off-the-land binary (e.g. regsvr32.exe, rundll32.exe, mshta.exe), also see T1218 (System Binary Proxy Execution) - Defense Evasion (TA0005).

blocks.text: EDR/antivirus signature or behavioral match on the executing process or the file hash; for LOLBin process names, detection typically comes from unusual parent-child process relationships (e.g. an Office app spawning regsvr32.exe) rather than the binary itself, since these are legitimate OS binaries being abused.
Capture the full process tree and the file hash; check the hash against a threat-intel feed to confirm it's a known family, not a false positive on a legitimate but unusually-invoked binary.

Isolate the affected endpoint from the network via EDR immediately - do not wait for full analysis to complete, since T1204.002 execution is frequently a precursor to further stages (C2 beaconing, lateral movement).
Remove the malicious file/process and any persistence mechanism it installed (scheduled tasks, run keys, services). Add the confirmed-malicious hash to the org-wide blocklist.
Reimage the endpoint if persistence mechanisms were found; if not, clean and monitor for 72 hours before returning it to normal use.

Record whether the delivery vector (attachment, drive-by, removable media) is a repeat pattern across incidents - if so, that vector's controls (attachment sandboxing, USB restrictions) need attention independent of this single case.

Email gateway/URL-reputation alert on an inbound link, or a user report of a suspicious message. Look for the T1566.002 indicators ATT&CK documents: mismatched sender/reply-to domains, lookalike/typosquatted domains, and URL-reputation or sandboxing engines flagging the destination.

Confirm whether the link was clicked and whether credentials were entered on the destination page (check email gateway click-tracking and, if available, proxy/DNS logs for the flagged domain). Determine scope: search for the same sender/domain/ subject across all mailboxes, not just the reporting user's.

Block the sender domain and the linked domain at the email gateway and web proxy/DNS layer. If any user clicked through, isolate that user's session (force logout) while the credential-compromise question in Analysis is resolved.
Quarantine or recall all matching messages org-wide. If credentials were entered, treat the account as compromised for eradication purposes, not just containment.
Force a password reset and MFA re-enrollment for any user who entered credentials; restore normal mail flow once the domain is blocked and matching messages are cleared.
Log whether this specific lure (sender pattern, domain, pretext) evaded existing email-gateway rules, and if so, tighten the matching rule rather than relying on user reporting alone next time.

/api/playbooks/privilege_escalation.name: privilege_escalation
/api/playbooks/privilege_escalation.title: Privilege Escalation
/api/playbooks/privilege_escalation.attack: this alert type covers three distinct scenarios, each with its own technique - cited separately rather than forced into one ID: - Added to a privileged group (e.g. Domain Admins) outside change management: T1098.007 (Account Manipulation: Additional Local or Domain Groups) - Privilege Escalation (TA0004). - Local exploit used to obtain SYSTEM access: T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation) - Privilege Escalation (TA0004). - Unapproved sudo/root access granted on Linux/macOS: T1548.003 (Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Sudo and Sudo Caching) - Privilege Escalation (TA0004).

blocks.text: Group-membership change audit log (T1098.007), an EDR alert on a known local privilege-escalation exploit pattern (T1068), or a sudoers/sudo-cache audit finding (T1548.003) - three different log sources depending on which scenario this is.

Confirm whether the elevated access was granted through an approved change ticket. If not, capture the process/command history that led to the escalation for root-cause analysis, and check for any additional accounts/groups modified in the same session.
Revoke the unapproved elevated access immediately.

Check the account/host for lateral movement or additional persistence mechanisms installed while elevated; if a local exploit was used (T1068), patch and reimage the host so the same exploit can't be reused.
Restore the account to its correct, pre-escalation permission level; verify no residual group memberships or sudo rules remain.

Close as Remediated if access was correctly reverted and no further compromise found; if this exposed a change-management gap (privileged group changes not requiring approval), fix that gap, not just this instance.

/api/playbooks/vulnerability.name: vulnerability
/api/playbooks/vulnerability.title: Vulnerability Management
/api/playbooks/vulnerability.attack: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application) - Initial Access (TA0001). Important scoping note: this alert type fires on an UNPATCHED, INTERNET-FACING vulnerability being found, not on a confirmed exploitation attempt - ATT&CK technique IDs describe observed adversary behavior, so T1190 here represents the technique an attacker WOULD use if this exposure is exploited, not something that has necessarily already happened.

blocks.text: Vulnerability scanner flags a CVE against an internet-facing asset.
Confirm CVSS score and whether a public exploit exists for this specific CVE - both materially change urgency versus a theoretical, unweaponized vulnerability.

If a public exploit exists and CVSS >= 9.0, apply a compensating control (WAF rule, network segmentation, or taking the service offline) immediately while a patch is prepared - do not leave a critical, actively-exploitable exposure live during patch scheduling.

Not typically applicable in the traditional sense (no confirmed compromise) unless exploitation is later confirmed, in which case treat as a fresh incident starting from whichever technique the exploit actually used.

Apply the vendor patch: within 48 hours for CVSS >= 9.0 on an internet-facing asset, within the next scheduled maintenance window (7 days) for CVSS 7.0-8.9. Verify the patch via rescan before closing.
If the same CVE recurs across multiple assets sharing a base image, fix the image and re-provision rather than patching each asset individually.

/api/playbooks/ddos.name: ddos
/api/playbooks/ddos.title: DDoS
/api/playbooks/ddos.attack: T1498 (Network Denial of Service) - Impact (TA0040). Where the traffic is a straightforward volumetric flood (not reflection/amplification), see sub-technique T1498.001 (Direct Network Flood) specifically.

blocks.text: CDN/upstream provider or internal monitoring flags a traffic-volume spike far above baseline, sourced from an unusually large or geographically dispersed set of IPs.

Confirm this is not a legitimate load event (marketing launch, viral traffic) before treating it as an attack - check the traffic-source pattern (organic referrers vs. uniform/scripted requests) and whether it targets a specific endpoint (e.g. login) rather than the site broadly, which points toward an application-layer attack rather than pure volumetric flood.

Enable upstream scrubbing/CDN rerouting for the affected service; for application-layer floods targeting a specific endpoint, add rate-limiting/CAPTCHA at that endpoint specifically rather than only at the network edge.
Not typically applicable in the traditional malware-removal sense - "eradication" here means confirming the flood source(s) are fully blocked/filtered, not just mitigated in effect.
Monitor service health until traffic returns to baseline; close as Mitigated once confirmed stable for 30 minutes.
If this targeted a specific endpoint rather than the whole service, add permanent rate-limiting there rather than relying on reactive scrubbing next time.
